newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Rubber pact due to go into force for 12 months.
newsitem.headline: Rubber pact due to go into force for 12 months.

text.p: A long-delayed price stabilisation pact for natural rubber is expected to be put into force on Thursday for 12 months, pending expected ratifications by China and Italy, U.N. sources said.

Exporting and importing countries are due to adopt a draft decision at a closed-door meeting in Geneva this morning, to be chaired by P.O. Thomas, of the Kuala-Lumpur based International Natural Rubber Organisation (INRO).
"The draft decision says they will put the agreement into force from today. It will be enforced on a provisional basis," a U.N. source told Reuters. "We expect a quick decision."
"The agreement says the situation has to be reviewed within 12 months by the International Natural Rubber Council," he said.
"The idea is that within 12 months everything is settled."

The 1995 International Natural Rubber Agreement stipulates that it can only enter into force once ratified by 80 per cent of both exporting and importing countries. But they may agree on a temporary entry-into-force if the average is 75 per cent.
Some 97.3 per cent of producer countries have ratified the stymied pact, including the world's five main producers -- Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Sri Lanka and Nigeria.
Leading importers have ratified the pact but only 73.4 per cent of importers have finalised their approval.

China (representing from eight to nine percent of imports) and Italy (three percent) have signed but have yet to ratify, according to sources at the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), which sponsored the negotiations.
The pact operates a buffer stock facility to stabilise prices. The maximum size of the buffer stocks remains 550,000 tonnes.
It is composed of the normal buffer stock of 400,000 tonnes with provision for an additional contingency buffer stock of 150,000 tonnes.
Producers and consumers share equally in financing the buffer stock, according to their respective trade shares.
The pact will have a duration of four years, with possibility of an extention of up to two years.
